rv.q: Whittaker proves more than up to the challenge with an enthrallingly layered take on the formidable Duchess.
Harris’s production has a campy TV movie panache that makes it very watchable, but that’s a bare minimum.

Shorn of the undercurrents of Webster's rich language, the extravagant violence – always hard to bring off and here translated into clever sonic torture and various gunnings-down – looks merely arbitrary.
The performances are powerful but the setup feels so overbearingly orchestrated that you do not feel the characters’ passion or anger.
However, The Duchess (of Malfi, as Webster had her) fails to convince from the start.
This production is fatally lacking in tragic richness and weight.
This update parks itself like a bus between the audience and the satanic masterpiece Webster actually wrote.

In Zinnie Harris’s dismal 2019 expurgation of Webster’s misogynist tragedy, Whittaker’s bland Duchess is held captive and murdered by her brothers. I’ve always struggled to make sense of the plot, but thanks to this I have — and wish I hadn’t. The incest angle is the torch carried for the Duchess by her twin Ferdinand (Rory Fleck Byrne).
It all adds up to less than the sum of its updated parts.
Long stretches feel like a rehearsal from a student production.
Harris keeps the characters around, becoming whispering consciences to the men who have none of their own – save for poor Antonio, of course.
Where Harris succeeds is in foregrounding the play’s sexual politics and drawing parallels with the present, from questions of ownership and coercion to pleasure and power.

Though Giovanna makes a stand against the way men treat her, Cariola and Julia, the Cardinal’s mistress, have even less chance to stand up against men, so it is left to their ghosts to wreak their revenge.
But for all its admirable boldness, there is something incongruous about seeing this early 17th century drama entirely rewritten for the modern day.
Whittaker makes a good stab at an impossible role, resisting her garrotting like a true pro, cursing like a trooper throughout.
In all, this show could do with a major rethink.
Zinnie Harris's 2019 incarnation of The Duchess of Malfi desperately yearns to conjure the sexy metatheatrical cunning of Van Hove, Mitchell, Ostermeier. It stumbles toe-curlingly at every hurdle.

cn.t: Critics find this modernized adaptation a muddled misfire that strips Webster's tragedy of its power. While Whittaker's performance earns praise, Harris's updated staging is deemed confusing, heavy-handed, and tonally off-balance.
